title: To Spain and Sindh
hookLine: Umayyad armies reach both Spain and the Indus, and a new world opens

cards: Boats push off from the North African shore and cross the narrow strait into Spain. Far to the east, troops march into Sindh, the lower Indus valley, in what is now Pakistan.
Two armies at opposite ends of one empire ruled from Damascus, sent out by different governors, in the same few years.
The histories date the crossing into Spain to the year ninety-two after the Hijra, which in the Christian calendar is 711. Today: to Spain and Sindh.

teach.b: In the west, the commander was Tariq ibn Ziyad, serving under Musa ibn Nusayr, the governor of North Africa.
Tariq crossed the strait, defeated the Visigothic king Roderic, and within a short time Muslim rule reached deep into the peninsula. The Arabic name for this new land was al-Andalus.
In the east, the commander was Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, sent by al-Hajjaj, the harsh governor of Iraq from Hasan al-Basri's story. He took the port of Daybul and defeated King Dahir of Sindh.

Call them what they were: conquests, with armies, sieges, people killed and captured. The histories that tell them were written by the winners' side, and they don't hide the fighting. But they also record what came after.

The historian al-Baladhuri reports that in Sindh, when the people of Brahmanabad asked to rebuild their temples and keep their worship, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim allowed it, treating their temples like the churches and synagogues of Christians and Jews, protected in return for a tax.
In al-Andalus, Christians and Jews also went on living under Muslim rule with that protected status.
Over time, both places grew their own Muslim cultures: al-Andalus with its scholars and cities, Sindh as an early door through which Islam entered South Asia.
An empire ruled from Damascus now touched the Atlantic and the Indus. So keep the number, but keep it whole: a year of war, and the start of long histories of neighbors. 711.

how: Muslims in Spain, Pakistan and India today sometimes trace their communities' stories back to these early arrivals, and historians read al-Baladhuri and other chronicles to reconstruct them.

practice: Bring to mind one place you know, your town, a city your family comes from, a country you'd like to see, and hold a question beside it: when did Muslims first arrive there, and how, by trade, by war, by marriage, by study?
You may not know, and that's fine. If you pray, remember the people of that place in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Andalus. The Muslim-ruled lands of Spain, reached by Umayyad armies in 711, the same years another army reached the Indus in Sindh. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Andalus, the name for the Muslim-ruled lands of the Iberian peninsula.

carryVoice: Your line: 711. Both ends of one empire moved in the same few years. See you tomorrow.
